opus-5.5.text:
No, I don't think you need closely matched examples. One of the more surprising things we've seen is how much generalization you get from fine-tuning. Pre-training gives the model an enormous amount of knowledge. It has seen the FFmpeg documentation, Stack Overflow threads, people's shell scripts, bug reports, all of that. What fine-tuning mostly does is teach the model a mode of behavior: you're an assistant, you take the user's request seriously, you try to produce something that actually works, you explain what you did.

Once the model has learned that behavior in some domains, it transfers pretty well to domains where you never gave it a single example. You might fine-tune on a bunch of general coding help in Python and some chat data, and then someone asks about an obscure FFmpeg filter graph, and the model just does the reasonable thing. It pulls the relevant knowledge from pre-training and puts it in the helpful-assistant format.

We saw something like this early on with multilingual behavior. If you fine-tune mostly on English instruction-following data, the model still behaves reasonably well as an assistant in other languages. The behavior generalizes across the language boundary, which suggests it's learning something fairly abstract rather than memorizing input-output pairs.

That said, matched data isn't useless. Where the details matter, like the exact flags, edge cases, or the quirks of a particular version, targeted data helps, especially for reliability. It also helps for anything requiring a particular style or workflow, like working inside a real environment, running commands, checking the output, and iterating. That's more than knowledge retrieval, and RL or demonstrations in that kind of setting make a big difference.

So I'd put it this way. The knowledge mostly comes from pre-training, and the behavior generalizes broadly from a relatively small amount of fine-tuning. Domain-specific data mostly polishes reliability. It isn't a prerequisite for the model to be useful at all.

fable-5.1.text:
No, I don't think you need closely matched examples at all. That's one of the things that surprised people when we were doing the early instruction-following work. If you train a model on a pretty small, generic set of demonstrations of helpful behavior, it generalizes way beyond the specific tasks in that set. So you might have a few hundred examples of answering questions or writing code, and then the model will happily help you with FFmpeg flags even if nothing like that showed up in the fine-tuning data.

The reason is that almost all the knowledge is already in the pretrained model. It's read the FFmpeg docs, it's read Stack Overflow threads where people are fighting with video encoding, it's seen tons of shell commands. What the fine-tuning is doing is more like telling the model which persona to adopt. Pretraining gives you a model that can imitate a huge range of documents and characters, and the supervised fine-tuning is a very cheap way of saying, "be the helpful assistant character, and answer the question directly rather than continuing the forum thread in some random direction." So you're steering, not teaching.

Where matched data does matter is more about format and quality calibration. If you want the model to produce a certain style, like showing the command and then explaining each flag, a few examples of that help a lot. And you can get into trouble if your fine-tuning data has a different knowledge profile than the model, where you're demonstrating answers the model doesn't actually know, and that can push it toward making things up. But the idea that you'd need an FFmpeg-specific dataset to get FFmpeg help, no, that's not how it works in practice. The generalization is the whole point.

astra-6.text:
No, I don’t think you need a closely matched supervised example. If the model has learned about FFmpeg during pretraining, it may already have the knowledge needed to answer the question. What fine-tuning needs to teach it is how to use that knowledge in response to a request—to act as an assistant.

So I’d distinguish learning the underlying capability from learning to elicit it. You might teach the assistant behavior with examples involving other programming tools, and have that generalize to FFmpeg. That doesn’t mean it will always get the command right, but you shouldn’t need a demonstration for every particular thing someone might ask about.

sol-6.1.text: I don’t think you need closely matched examples. A model can learn a lot about FFmpeg from pretraining—what the commands do, how people use them—and then supervised fine-tuning can teach it how to use that knowledge in a conversation. So you don’t necessarily need an example of someone asking the particular FFmpeg question you care about. You need the model to generalize from the instruction-following examples to knowledge it already has. And that generalization seems to work pretty well, although it’s certainly not perfect.
